questions.q: In the Brightfield Retail scenario, how was the contractor's database access originally granted?
options: By role-copying — mirroring another team's permissions — instead of scoping access to the actual dashboard task
Through a formal least-privilege review scoped to the dashboard task
It was never granted at all, which was the actual failure
Through a one-time, automatically expiring temporary credential
questions.explain: Access was granted as 'give them what the analytics team has' rather than scoped to what the dashboard work actually required — a classic role-copying failure covered in Chapter 3.

questions.q: Why did the contractor's database login remain active for three months after the contract ended?
options: No single system or owner was responsible for the step of revoking database access during offboarding
The company's policy required logins to remain active for a mandatory grace period
The contractor had legitimate ongoing business need for the access
Database access was automatically renewed by the analytics platform
questions.explain: Payroll and badge access were shut off on schedule, but database access revocation had no named owner in the offboarding checklist, so it silently didn't happen.

questions.q: What ultimately detected the dormant login's activity in this scenario?
options: An unrelated periodic access review that surfaced the still-active login querying customer data
A customer complaint filed directly with the regulator
An automated encryption key rotation process
The contractor self-reported the access after the contract ended
questions.explain: The incident was caught during an unrelated access review, which is exactly the kind of catch a periodic review process and a well-formed audit log are meant to enable.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what two Chapter 4 protections could have reduced the exposure even with the access already granted?
options: Masking the payment-card fragment and applying row-level security to limit queries to aggregated totals
Deleting the customer_orders table entirely and encrypting all backups
Requiring two-factor authentication only for the contractor's account
Changing the contractor's job title in the HR system
questions.explain: Masking sensitive fields for a reporting-only login, or using row-level security to limit visibility to aggregated regional totals, would have reduced the exposure even without fixing the underlying access-grant problem.

questions.q: What does this case study conclude about why the Brightfield incident was able to happen?
options: It required gaps in four different chapters' worth of controls lining up at once, not one single dramatic failure
It happened purely because the contractor acted maliciously
It happened because Brightfield had no security team at all
It was caused entirely by a software bug in the database engine
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as a compounding control failure — classification, access control, data protection, and the lifecycle/logging gaps all had to line up for the incident to occur and go unnoticed for months.
